title: Korean Lunar New Year Seollal: A Salaryman's Honest Take
tldr: Korean Lunar New Year, or Seollal, is primarily about ancestral reverence and reaffirming family ties, not just gifts.
It's a significant financial and logistical challenge for many Koreans, involving expensive gifts, 'sebaetdon,' and grueling travel.
While traditions like 'charye' and 'tteokguk' remain central, modern Seollal is evolving with more people opting for personal breaks or overseas travel.
target_audience: This is for readers who want to understand the deeper cultural significance and practical realities of Korean Lunar New Year beyond tourist guides.
content:
📅 Updated 2026.10.02
Key takeaways
  • Korean Lunar New Year, or Seollal, is primarily about ancestral reverence and reaffirming family ties, not just gifts.
  • It's a significant financial and logistical challenge for many Koreans, involving expensive gifts, 'sebaetdon,' and grueling travel.
  • While traditions like 'charye' and 'tteokguk' remain central, modern Seollal is evolving with more people opting for personal breaks or overseas travel.
👤 This is for readers who want to understand the deeper cultural significance and practical realities of Korean Lunar New Year beyond tourist guides.

You've probably heard of Seollal, the Korean Lunar New Year, and might picture a joyous family gathering with lots of food and gifts. And yes, it is that, but honestly, it’s also one of the most exhausting, expensive, and logistically challenging times of the year for most Koreans, myself included. As of October 01, 2026, it remains a cornerstone of our culture, yet its practice is subtly shifting, revealing the underlying pressures and changing social dynamics. It's much more than just a holiday; it's a deep dive into what being Korean really means.

Seollal Explained: More Than Just “Happy New Year”

At its core, Seollal (Korean Lunar New Year) is our most important traditional holiday, marking the beginning of a new year on the lunar calendar. It's not just a secular celebration; it's profoundly spiritual, centered around honoring ancestors and solidifying family bonds. The main event, the charye (ancestral rites), happens first. This is where we gather, usually at the eldest son's home, to formally pay respects to our ancestors with an elaborate table of food. It's a solemn, quiet ritual, a moment of deep connection to the past. After charye, we perform sebae (a formal deep bow to elders), and in return, the elders offer sebaetdon (new year's money) and words of blessing. I still remember the thrill of getting my first 10,000 won as a kid after bowing to my grandparents. Now, as an adult, I'm on the giving end, and it’s a whole different kind of thrill… or financial pressure.

Point: Seollal is less about partying and more about reverence, tradition, and reinforcing the family hierarchy, tying us directly to our lineage.

The Real Cost of Korean Lunar New Year: Your Wallet Takes a Hit

Let’s be honest, Seollal is expensive. It's a significant financial drain for families across the country. The biggest costs come from sebaetdon and gifts. For sebaetdon, a typical amount for a young child might be 30,000-50,000 won (roughly $22-$37 USD, depending on the current exchange rate), while teenagers might get 50,000-100,000 won. If you have several nieces, nephews, and younger cousins, that adds up fast. I usually budget around 500,000 won just for sebaetdon alone. Then there are the gifts. It’s customary to bring thoughtful presents for your parents, in-laws, and other relatives. These often include expensive health supplements like red ginseng, high-quality beef sets, fruit gift boxes, or department store gift certificates. A decent beef set can easily run you 200,000-300,000 won (around $150-$220 USD). My company gives us a holiday bonus, but honestly, most of it goes straight out the door to cover Seollal expenses. It’s a cultural expectation, and failing to meet it would be a huge loss of nunchi (the art of reading the room) and a source of silent judgment.

Point: Seollal is a cultural necessity, but it comes with a hefty price tag that most Koreans silently endure as part of their duty.

Navigating the Seollal Migration: Traffic, Trains, and Tensions

Imagine half the country trying to go home at the exact same time – that’s Seollal travel. The mass exodus, known as gwi-seong (returning home for the holidays), turns expressways into parking lots. A trip that normally takes three hours can stretch to ten or twelve. Many people try to secure KTX (Korea Train eXpress) tickets, but they sell out in minutes after booking opens. I once stayed up until midnight, multiple devices open, just to snag a ticket, only to fail. Since then, my family usually drives, and I swear, every year I vow never to do it again. Besides the physical exhaustion of travel, there's the emotional labor. Extended family gatherings can be wonderful, but they also mean navigating complex family dynamics, dealing with intrusive questions about marriage or career, and the general stress of being in close quarters for days. My coworker swears he goes straight to a PC bang (internet café) for a few hours just to decompress after getting home from his parents' house.

Point: The journey to Seollal is an annual pilgrimage fraught with logistical headaches and social pressures, making the 'holiday' feel more like an endurance test.

Seollal Food: Beyond Tteokguk and the Labor Behind It

Everyone knows tteokguk (rice cake soup) for Seollal – eating it traditionally means you've officially turned a year older. But the Seollal feast extends far beyond that. The charye table alone requires a huge variety of dishes: jeon (savory pancakes like dongtaejeon made with pollock or hobakjeon with zucchini), galbijjim (braised short ribs), japchae (glass noodles with vegetables), and various namul (seasoned vegetables). Preparing all this food is an immense undertaking, traditionally falling mostly on the women of the family. My mom and aunts start cooking days in advance. I usually help with some chopping and dishwashing, but it's nothing compared to their effort. This collective effort, while tiring, is also a form of bonding and an expression of love. Honestly, by the time we actually sit down to eat, everyone's exhausted but immensely proud of the spread. It’s also when the biggest family arguments sometimes break out, usually about who’s doing what and why this vegetable isn’t cut correctly.

Point: Seollal food is a delicious symbol of abundance and tradition, but it represents days of intensive labor, often disproportionately shouldered by family women.

Modern Seollal: Changing Traditions and New Realities

While the core values of Seollal persist, the way Koreans celebrate is definitely evolving, especially among younger generations. As of 2026, we see a growing trend of people opting out of the traditional mass family gathering. Some choose to travel overseas, using the long holiday break for a personal vacation rather than family obligations. Others opt for a 'reverse Seollal,' where parents visit their children in the city, or families meet at a neutral location like a restaurant or a hotel. There's even a term, myeongjeol ihon (holiday divorce), for the spike in divorce filings after the major holidays due to accumulated family stress. My company now offers an optional 'Seollal travel stipend' instead of a traditional gift set, which many of my colleagues take to book a quick trip to Jeju or even Japan. It’s a quiet rebellion against the pressure, a sign that while tradition is important, personal well-being and choice are gaining ground.

Point: Modern Seollal is seeing a shift from rigid tradition to more flexible, individual-centric celebrations, reflecting broader societal changes and personal priorities.

The things that trip people up

Q. What is the primary purpose of Seollal?

A. The primary purpose of Seollal is to honor ancestors through traditional rites called *charye* and to strengthen family bonds by gathering and showing respect to elders, often through *sebae*.

Q. What are some significant costs associated with Seollal?

A. Significant costs for Seollal include *sebaetdon* (new year's money) given to younger relatives, expensive gifts like high-quality beef or health supplements for elders, and often substantial travel expenses.

Q. How do Koreans typically travel during Seollal?

A. Koreans typically travel long distances during Seollal by car, leading to severe traffic jams, or by high-speed trains like the KTX, for which tickets are notoriously difficult to secure due to high demand.

Q. What food is most commonly eaten on Seollal?

A. The most iconic food for Seollal is *tteokguk* (rice cake soup), as traditionally, eating it signifies gaining another year of age; however, elaborate feasts with various *jeon*, *galbijjim*, and *japchae* are also prepared.

Q. Are Seollal traditions changing in modern Korea?

A. Yes, Seollal traditions are evolving; more Koreans, especially younger generations, are choosing to travel overseas or have smaller, more personal gatherings instead of the traditional large family reunions, reflecting a shift in priorities.

한국 설날: 한 직장인의 솔직한 이야기

여러분은 아마 한국의 설날에 대해 들어보셨을 것이고, 많은 음식과 선물로 가득한 즐거운 가족 모임을 상상하실지도 모릅니다. 네, 맞습니다. 하지만 솔직히 말해서, 저를 포함한 대부분의 한국인에게 설날은 한 해 중 가장 힘들고, 비싸고, 물류적으로 어려운 시기 중 하나이기도 합니다. 2026년 10월 1일 현재, 설날은 우리 문화의 초석으로 남아있지만, 그 관행은 미묘하게 변화하고 있으며, 이는 근본적인 압력과 변화하는 사회 역학을 보여줍니다. 설날은 단순한 휴일 그 이상입니다. 그것은 한국인이라는 것이 진정으로 무엇을 의미하는지에 대한 깊은 탐구입니다.

## 설날 설명: "새해 복 많이 받으세요" 그 이상

설날(한국 음력 설날)은 음력으로 새해를 알리는 우리의 가장 중요한 전통 명절입니다. 세속적인 축하 행사가 아니라, 조상을 기리고 가족 유대를 강화하는 데 중점을 둔 깊이 있는 정신적인 의미를 지닙니다. 주요 행사인 차례(조상 제사)가 먼저 진행됩니다. 이때 우리는 보통 장남의 집에 모여 정성껏 차려진 음식상으로 조상께 정식으로 예를 표합니다. 엄숙하고 조용한 의식이며, 과거와의 깊은 연결의 순간입니다. 차례 후에는 세배(어른께 정식으로 큰절)를 드리고, 그 대가로 어른들은 세뱃돈과 덕담을 주십니다. 어렸을 때 할머니, 할아버지께 절하고 처음으로 10,000원을 받았을 때의 설렘이 아직도 기억납니다. 이제 어른이 되어 주는 입장이 되었는데, 이것은 완전히 다른 종류의 설렘… 또는 재정적 압박입니다.

> 요점: 설날은 파티보다는 경건함, 전통, 그리고 가족 위계를 강화하는 데 중점을 두며, 우리를 우리의 혈통과 직접적으로 연결합니다.

## 한국 설날의 실제 비용: 지갑에 타격

솔직히 말해서, 설날은 비쌉니다. 전국 가족들에게 상당한 재정적 부담이 됩니다. 가장 큰 비용은 세뱃돈과 선물에서 나옵니다. 세뱃돈의 경우, 어린아이에게는 보통 30,000~50,000원(현재 환율에 따라 약 22~37달러) 정도이고, 십대에게는 50,000~100,000원 정도입니다. 조카, 조카딸, 어린 사촌들이 여러 명 있다면 그 금액은 빠르게 늘어납니다. 저는 보통 세뱃돈만으로 약 500,000원을 예산으로 잡습니다. 그리고 선물도 있습니다. 부모님, 시부모님, 다른 친척들에게 정성껏 준비한 선물을 드리는 것이 관례입니다. 여기에는 종종 홍삼과 같은 값비싼 건강 보조 식품, 고급 한우 세트, 과일 선물 상자, 또는 백화점 상품권이 포함됩니다. 괜찮은 한우 세트는 쉽게 200,000~300,000원(약 150~220달러)이 들 수 있습니다. 저희 회사에서는 명절 보너스를 주지만, 솔직히 대부분은 설날 비용을 충당하는 데 바로 나갑니다. 이것은 문화적 기대이며, 이를 충족시키지 못하면 엄청난 눈치 손실과 조용한 비난의 원인이 될 것입니다.

> 요점: 설날은 문화적 필수 요소이지만, 대부분의 한국인이 의무의 일부로 묵묵히 감당하는 상당한 비용이 따릅니다.

## 설날 이동: 교통 체증, 기차, 그리고 긴장

나라의 절반이 동시에 집으로 가려고 한다고 상상해 보세요. 그것이 설날 이동입니다. 귀성(명절에 집으로 돌아가는 것)으로 알려진 대규모 이동은 고속도로를 주차장으로 만듭니다. 평소 3시간 걸리는 여행이 10시간 또는 12시간으로 늘어날 수 있습니다. 많은 사람들이 KTX(한국고속철도) 티켓을 확보하려고 하지만, 예매가 시작된 지 몇 분 만에 매진됩니다. 저는 한 번은 자정까지 여러 기기를 켜놓고 티켓을 잡으려고 했지만 실패했습니다. 그 이후로 저희 가족은 보통 차를 운전하는데, 맹세컨대 매년 다시는 하지 않겠다고 다짐합니다. 여행의 육체적 피로 외에도 감정적 노동이 있습니다. 대가족 모임은 훌륭할 수 있지만, 복잡한 가족 역학을 헤쳐나가고, 결혼이나 직업에 대한 간섭적인 질문에 대처하며, 며칠 동안 가까이 지내는 일반적인 스트레스를 의미하기도 합니다. 제 동료는 부모님 댁에서 돌아온 후 긴장을 풀기 위해 몇 시간 동안 PC방(인터넷 카페)으로 직행한다고 맹세합니다.

> 요점: 설날로 가는 여정은 물류적 어려움과 사회적 압력으로 가득 찬 연례 순례이며, '휴일'을 인내심 테스트처럼 느끼게 합니다.

## 설날 음식: 떡국 그 이상, 그리고 그 뒤에 숨겨진 노동

모두가 설날 떡국을 압니다. 떡국을 먹는 것은 전통적으로 한 살 더 먹는다는 것을 의미합니다. 하지만 설날 잔치는 그 이상으로 확장됩니다. 차례상만 해도 동태전이나 호박전 같은 다양한 전, 갈비찜, 잡채, 그리고 다양한 나물 등 엄청난 종류의 음식이 필요합니다. 이 모든 음식을 준비하는 것은 엄청난 일이며, 전통적으로 가족의 여성들에게 주로 돌아갑니다. 저희 엄마와 이모들은 며칠 전부터 요리를 시작합니다. 저는 보통 채소 썰기나 설거지를 돕지만, 그들의 노력에 비하면 아무것도 아닙니다. 이 공동의 노력은 피곤하지만, 유대감을 형성하고 사랑을 표현하는 형태이기도 합니다. 솔직히, 실제로 식탁에 앉을 때쯤이면 모두 지쳐 있지만, 차려진 음식에 엄청난 자부심을 느낍니다. 이때 가장 큰 가족 싸움이 터지기도 하는데, 보통 누가 무엇을 하고 왜 이 채소가 제대로 썰리지 않았는지에 대한 것입니다.

> 요점: 설날 음식은 풍요와 전통의 맛있는 상징이지만, 며칠간의 고된 노동을 의미하며, 종종 가족 여성들이 불균형하게 감당합니다.

## 현대 설날: 변화하는 전통과 새로운 현실

설날의 핵심 가치는 지속되지만, 한국인들이 설날을 기념하는 방식은 특히 젊은 세대 사이에서 분명히 진화하고 있습니다. 2026년 현재, 전통적인 대가족 모임에서 벗어나려는 사람들이 늘고 있습니다. 일부는 긴 연휴를 가족 의무 대신 개인 휴가를 위해 해외여행을 선택합니다. 다른 사람들은 '역귀성'을 선택하여 부모님이 도시의 자녀를 방문하거나, 가족들이 식당이나 호텔과 같은 중립적인 장소에서 만납니다. 심지어 누적된 가족 스트레스로 인해 주요 명절 이후 이혼 신청이 급증하는 현상을 나타내는 '명절 이혼'이라는 용어도 있습니다. 저희 회사는 이제 전통적인 선물 세트 대신 선택적인 '설날 여행 지원금'을 제공하는데, 많은 동료들이 제주도나 심지어 일본으로 짧은 여행을 예약하는 데 사용합니다. 이것은 압력에 대한 조용한 반항이며, 전통이 중요하지만 개인의 안녕과 선택이 중요성을 얻고 있다는 신호입니다.

> 요점: 현대 설날은 엄격한 전통에서 벗어나 보다 유연하고 개인 중심적인 축하 방식으로 변화하고 있으며, 이는 광범위한 사회 변화와 개인의 우선순위를 반영합니다.

A trip that normally takes three hours can stretch to ten or twelve. Many people try to secure KTX (Korea Train eXpress) tickets, but they sell out in minutes after booking opens. I once stayed up until midnight, multiple devices open, just to snag a ticket, only to fail. Since then, my family usually drives, and I swear, every year I vow never to do it again. Besides the physical exhaustion of travel, there's the emotional labor. Extended family gatherings can be wonderful, but they also mean navigating complex family dynamics, dealing with intrusive questions about marriage or career, and the general stress of being in close quarters for days. My coworker swears he goes straight to a PC bang (internet café) for a few hours just to decompress after getting home from his parents' house.

> Point: The journey to Seollal is an annual pilgrimage fraught with logistical headaches and social pressures, making the 'holiday' feel more like an endurance test.

## Seollal Food: Beyond Tteokguk and the Labor Behind It

Everyone knows tteokguk (rice cake soup) for Seollal – eating it traditionally means you've officially turned a year older. But the Seollal feast extends far beyond that. The charye table alone requires a huge variety of dishes: jeon (savory pancakes like dongtaejeon made with pollock or hobakjeon with zucchini), galbijjim (braised short ribs), japchae (glass noodles with vegetables), and various namul (seasoned vegetables). Preparing all this food is an immense undertaking, traditionally falling mostly on the women of the family. My mom and aunts start cooking days in advance. I usually help with some chopping and dishwashing, but it's nothing compared to their effort. This collective effort, while tiring, is also a form of bonding and an expression of love. Honestly, by the time we actually sit down to eat, everyone's exhausted but immensely proud of the spread. It’s also when the biggest family arguments sometimes break out, usually about who’s doing what and why this vegetable isn’t cut correctly.

> Point: Seollal food is a delicious symbol of abundance and tradition, but it represents days of intensive labor, often disproportionately shouldered by family women.

## Modern Seollal: Changing Traditions and New Realities

While the core values of Seollal persist, the way Koreans celebrate is definitely evolving, especially among younger generations. As of 2026, we see a growing trend of people opting out of the traditional mass family gathering. Some choose to travel overseas, using the long holiday break for a personal vacation rather than family obligations. Others opt for a 'reverse Seollal,' where parents visit their children in the city, or families meet at a neutral location like a restaurant or a hotel. There's even a term, myeongjeol ihon (holiday divorce), for the spike in divorce filings after the major holidays due to accumulated family stress. My company now offers an optional 'Seollal travel stipend' instead of a traditional gift set, which many of my colleagues take to book a quick trip to Jeju or even Japan. It’s a quiet rebellion against the pressure, a sign that while tradition is important, personal well-being and choice are gaining ground.

> Point: Modern Seollal is seeing a shift from rigid tradition to more flexible, individual-centric celebrations, reflecting broader societal changes and personal priorities.

mainEntity.name: What is the primary purpose of Seollal?

acceptedAnswer.text: The primary purpose of Seollal is to honor ancestors through traditional rites called *charye* and to strengthen family bonds by gathering and showing respect to elders, often through *sebae*.

mainEntity.name: What are some significant costs associated with Seollal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Significant costs for Seollal include *sebaetdon* (new year's money) given to younger relatives, expensive gifts like high-quality beef or health supplements for elders, and often substantial travel expenses.

mainEntity.name: How do Koreans typically travel during Seollal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Koreans typically travel long distances during Seollal by car, leading to severe traffic jams, or by high-speed trains like the KTX, for which tickets are notoriously difficult to secure due to high demand.

mainEntity.name: What food is most commonly eaten on Seollal?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most iconic food for Seollal is *tteokguk* (rice cake soup), as traditionally, eating it signifies gaining another year of age; however, elaborate feasts with various *jeon*, *galbijjim*, and *japchae* are also prepared.

mainEntity.name: Are Seollal traditions changing in modern Korea?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, Seollal traditions are evolving; more Koreans, especially younger generations, are choosing to travel overseas or have smaller, more personal gatherings instead of the traditional large family reunions, reflecting a shift in priorities.
